clinicalPearls: In-toeing is one of the commonest reasons for orthopaedic referral in childhood and is usually a normal variant that provokes more parental than functional concern

The three anatomical levels responsible are the foot (metatarsus adductus), the leg (internal tibial torsion), and the hip (increased femoral anteversion), and each predominates at a characteristic age
Metatarsus adductus dominates in infancy, internal tibial torsion in the toddler, and femoral anteversion in the older preschool and early school child
A systematic rotational profile with the foot progression angle localises the level of the deformity and guides counselling
The great majority of cases are physiological, symmetrical, painless, and resolve spontaneously as the skeleton matures
Reassurance and periodic observation are the mainstays, and orthotics, special shoes, braces, and exercises do not alter the natural history
Surgery is exceptional and reserved for severe, persistent, functionally significant torsional deformity in the older child
reference.pathophysiology: In-toeing is a symptom rather than a single disease, describing an inwardly directed foot progression angle during gait that arises from rotational alignment at one or more levels of the lower limb. Most commonly it reflects the normal sequence of skeletal maturation, in which fetal internal torsion of the tibia and high femoral anteversion gradually derotate through childhood; a lag in this process leaves a residual inward rotation. At the foot, medial deviation of the metatarsals in metatarsus adductus contributes. Pathological in-toeing is uncommon and is largely confined to neuromuscular conditions such as cerebral palsy, in which spasticity and failure of physiological derotation maintain the inward gait.
additionalDifferentials: Neuromuscular gait disorder such as cerebral palsy
Developmental dysplasia of the hip altering rotation
additionalInvestigations: Full rotational profile including foot progression angle, hip rotation, thigh-foot angle, and foot shape
Trochanteric prominence (Craig) test for femoral anteversion
Observation of the child walking and running to characterise the gait
Examination of the feet for metatarsus adductus and of the hips for dysplasia
Standing lower-limb radiographs only if angular deformity or pathology is suspected
Rotational computed tomography reserved for preoperative planning in severe cases
redFlags: Progressive deformity rather than the expected improvement with growth
Neurological signs suggesting cerebral palsy or another neuromuscular disorder
Short stature or dysmorphism suggesting a skeletal dysplasia
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent, with spontaneous resolution in the overwhelming majority as the tibia and femur derotate with growth, and normal function without arthritic consequence is the expected outcome for physiological in-toeing.
pitfalls: Treating a benign variant with ineffective braces, cables, or special footwear
Failing to localise the level of the deformity with a proper rotational profile
Overlooking asymmetry, pain, or neurological signs that point to a pathological cause
Recommending surgery prematurely before natural derotation is complete
Providing reassurance without arranging follow-up when the presentation is atypical
references: Staheli LT, rotational problems of the lower extremity
management: Reassurance and parental education that physiological in-toeing is a normal variant that resolves with skeletal maturation
Periodic observation with serial rotational-profile assessment to confirm spontaneous derotation
Avoidance of orthotics, corrective shoes, braces and exercises, which do not alter the natural history
Referral for orthopaedic assessment where features are atypical, such as pain, marked asymmetry, progressive deformity or signs of a neuromuscular disorder
Management of any underlying neuromuscular cause such as cerebral palsy, including spasticity treatment and physiotherapy
Rotational osteotomy reserved for severe, persistent deformity causing functional or cosmetic problems in the older child
